# Global Supply Chain Resilience & Responsible Sourcing
## Map the network before you buy the buffer

---

## 0. Three decisions before anything is designed

1. **Resilience is purchased, not exhorted — and the procurement scorecard decides whether it happens.** If purchase price variance and unit cost remain the dominant measures of buyer performance, every dual-source commitment, every capacity reservation and every audit finding will be quietly traded away at the next negotiation. Change the incentive first. A resilience programme laid over an unchanged cost scorecard is theatre with a budget line.
2. **Ethics and resilience are one programme, not two.** They share a root cause: opaque, concentrated, price-squeezed sourcing from nodes you have no relationship with and cannot see. They share a data spine: one supplier master, one *site-level* map, one risk register. Run them as separate functions and you will pay twice for the same mapping work and still be surprised twice.
3. **You are a cause of your own supply risk.** Engineering creates most sole sources at design release, not procurement in negotiation. And your own purchasing practices — orders placed inside the frozen window, lead times below the agreed minimum, prices below the cost of legal compliance, late payment — are what generate the forced overtime and unauthorised subcontracting your auditors later "discover." Externalising this to suppliers is comfortable and wrong.

---

## 1. Unbundle: "supply chain risk" is five different problems with five different instruments

| | **Node failure** | **Link failure** | **Systemic / geopolitical** | **Ethical & regulatory** | **Cyber & data** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Example** | Supplier fire, insolvency, quality stop, strike | Port congestion, canal closure, freight capacity, customs | Export controls, sanctions, tariffs, conflict, pandemic | Forced labour, wage theft, unauthorised subcontracting, deforestation | Supplier ransomware halting their plant or leaking your BOM |
| **Signature** | Single-supplier, idiosyncratic, sudden | Route-correlated, affects many suppliers at once | Country- or bloc-correlated, slow onset then step change | Long latent, then binary: detention, injunction, deselection | Sudden, opaque, supplier reluctant to disclose |
| **Wrong instrument** | Inventory everywhere | A second supplier in the same cluster | Nearshoring as ideology | More audits | Contract clause with no verification |
| **Right instrument** | Qualified live second source; tooling ownership; financial monitoring | Multi-modal, multi-port, inventory positioned at the commonality point | Site-level geographic diversification; scenario-tested legal exposure | Sub-tier traceability, worker voice, purchasing-practice reform | Supplier security tiering, recovery-time commitments, tested |
| **Cost** | Moderate, part-specific | Low–moderate | High, structural | Low–moderate, high coordination | Low |

**The critical connection:** all five are invisible until you have a **site-level, sub-tier map of the parts that can stop your lines.** Every instrument above requires it. This is why mapping is not phase one of the programme — it *is* the programme's precondition, and it is the cheapest thing on the list.

---

## 2. The diagnostic that requires no probability estimates

Stop trying to forecast disruptions. You cannot. Instead, for each node ask two questions that have knowable answers:

- **TTR — Time to Recover:** if this site stopped today, how long until supply is restored (from this site, or from a qualified alternative that has actually shipped)?
- **TTS — Time to Survive:** how long can we keep producing without it, given inventory in the whole chain?

**Exposure is the gap.** Where TTS ≥ TTR, you are covered and should spend nothing more. Where TTR exceeds TTS, you have a quantified, defensible number.

*Illustrative; substitute actuals.*

| Node | TTR | TTS | Gap | Revenue at risk | Marginal cost to close |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom IC, sole foundry | 52 wks | 8 wks | 44 wks | €31m | High — redesign or long buffer |
| Connector, single site, one region | 26 wks | 3 wks | 23 wks | €18m | Low — second source exists, needs qualification |
| Casting, "two suppliers" — same foundry cluster, same port | 14 wks | 6 wks | 8 wks | €9m | Low — geographic re-split |
| Fastener, three suppliers, three regions | 4 wks | 12 wks | — | — | Nothing. Stop managing it. |

Then rank by **cost per week of exposure removed** and buy from the top. This replaces the two standard failure modes — a blanket inventory increase across everything, and a heroic dual-sourcing mandate on the highest-spend items — with a defensible spending sequence. Note the pattern in almost every real network: **the parts that stop you are cheap.** A €0.40 connector halts a €40,000 machine. Spend-based supplier segmentation systematically misses them.

**The diversity illusion test.** Before believing any diversification claim, collapse your supplier list four ways: by ultimate parent, by *manufacturing site*, by shared sub-tier input, and by port of exit. Apparent diversity usually collapses to one or two real nodes. Run this before you fund anything.

---

## 3. Price the status quo, including the ethical tail

| | |
|---|---|
| Line-stop contribution loss per day | €250k |
| Disruption events causing ≥3-day stoppage, trailing 3-yr average | 1.4 / yr |
| Average duration | 6 days → **~€2.1m/yr** |
| Expedite freight, premium spot buys, redesign firefighting | **+€0.9m/yr** |
| Annual imports of inputs exposed to rebuttable-presumption import bans | €40m |
| One border detention: 6 weeks of supply held + line stop + retro-traceability | **€4–6m, single event** |
| Cost of a pre-assembled traceability pack for those inputs | ~€300k once, then maintenance |

Two conclusions the board needs in one slide. First, the recurring disruption cost is already being paid — it is just booked as expedite freight and missed shipments rather than as a resilience gap. Second, **ethical exposure is not a reputational abstraction; it is a binary cash event at a border**, and traceability is cheap insurance priced against it. Regulation has converted ethics from a values question into a customs and liability question, which is why it now competes for capital successfully.

---

## 4. The intervention ladder — climb it in order

| Tier | Content | Cost | Time to effect | Reversibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — See it** | BOM→supplier→**site** mapping; sub-tier discovery for critical parts; TTR/TTS on top 100 nodes; single-point-of-failure register; diversity-illusion collapse; supplier financial-health monitoring | Near-zero capex, high coordination | 2–4 months | Total |
| **0b — Engineer it out** | Part standardisation and commonality; remove spec-locked sole sources; approve alternates in the drawing; design-for-substitutability on new programmes | Low, engineering time | 3–12 months | Total |
| **1 — Contract for it** | Sub-tier disclosure obligations; right to unannounced audit including sub-tier; capacity reservation; tooling ownership and escrow; minimum lead-time and frozen-window commitments *both ways*; insolvency early-warning triggers; cyber recovery-time commitments | Low | 2–6 months | High |
| **2 — Physically hedge it** | Qualified second sources with a **live volume split** (e.g. 75/25) in a different region; strategic buffer positioned at the commonality point, not everywhere; multi-modal and multi-port routing; regional finished-goods positioning | Moderate opex + working capital | 4–12 months | High |
| **3 — Restructure it** | Selective regionalisation on a per-part calculation; in-house capability for the genuinely irreplaceable; long-term offtake or JV on scarce inputs; supplier development to create a second source where none exists | High capex | 12–36 months | Low |

**Design rules.** Tier 0 and 0b are mandatory and unconditional. Never fund Tier 2 or 3 for a node whose Tier 0b option has not been examined — **the cheapest resilience is an approved alternate part number, and it is free.** A second source that has not shipped in the last 90 days is not a second source; it is a document. And never split volume so thinly that neither supplier will hold capacity for you.

---

## 5. Responsible sourcing: retire audit theatre

The standard programme — a signed code of conduct, an announced annual audit, a corrective action plan, a spreadsheet of completion percentages — reliably detects fire exits and reliably misses forced labour, wage theft and freedom-of-association violations. It is optimised to produce evidence of effort, not evidence of conditions.

**What actually detects abuse:**

- **Worker voice the supplier does not control.** A grievance channel reached from a personal phone, in the migrant workforce's own languages, operated by a third party, with case closure confirmed *by the worker*, not the factory. This is the single highest-yield instrument available and it costs a fraction of an audit programme.
- **Recruitment-fee mapping.** For any site using migrant labour, trace the labour agents and who paid what. Recruitment debt is the mechanism of most modern forced labour. If you cannot name the agents, you do not know your risk.
- **Wage verification against bank records**, not the factory's ledger. Payroll books are the most-rehearsed document in any facility.
- **Unannounced, worker-interview-led assessment** with off-site interviews. Announced audits measure preparation.
- **Sub-tier and subcontractor discovery.** Unauthorised subcontracting is where the worst conditions sit, and it is usually a direct response to a purchase order the supplier could not legally fulfil.
- **Traceability to origin for regulated inputs** — cotton, polysilicon, cobalt, mica, timber, palm, tin/tantalum/tungsten/gold, fish. Documentary chain of custody, pre-assembled, with lab or isotopic verification where it exists. Assemble it before a border officer asks, not after.

**Reform your own purchasing practices.** Measure and publish internally: percentage of orders changed inside the frozen window, percentage of POs issued below the agreed minimum lead time, on-time payment rate, and whether the price supports the legal minimum wage plus statutory overtime in that jurisdiction. If these are bad, your audit findings are self-inflicted and remediation will not stick.

**Remediate; exit only for refusal.** Cut-and-run on a finding punishes the workers, destroys your visibility, and moves the problem to a supplier you cannot see. Reserve termination for zero-tolerance findings and for refusal to remediate against a dated plan. Fund
